did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with the title “For the director: al nehilot, a psalm of David,” and is presented as a psalm attributed to David. The meaning of the word “nehilot” is not explained in the psalm itself.
The poet asks the Lord to listen to three dimensions of his prayer: “my words,” “my thoughts,” and “the sound of my cry.”
The title “My King and my God” expresses the poet’s faith that the Lord is both his king and the God to whom he turns in prayer.
The poet describes a morning routine of prayer: “In the morning you hear my voice,” and “in the morning I lay my requests before you”; afterward, he waits expectantly for an answer.
The psalm presents a clear contrast between the Lord and the wicked: the Lord does not delight in wickedness, and evil cannot dwell in his presence.
These verses list several types of evildoers whom the Lord rejects: the arrogant, those who practice wrongdoing, liars, bloodthirsty people, and deceitful people.
The poet emphasizes that he enters the Lord’s house not by his own merit alone, but “because of your abundant kindness”; he enters with bowing and reverence.
The poet asks the Lord to guide him on a straight path precisely in the face of his enemies, linking the prayer for guidance with the struggle against opposition and danger.
The description of the wicked uses powerful images of deceptive speech: there is no truth in their mouths, their throats are like open graves, and their tongues speak flattering words.
Toward the end, the tone shifts from a request for protection to joy: those who take refuge in the Lord and love his name are described as singing and rejoicing because the Lord protects them.
The image “With favor you surround him as with a shield” portrays the Lord’s favor as a shield surrounding the righteous. Thus, the psalm ends with blessing, protection, and closeness to the Lord.
